newsitem.title: JAPAN: High zinc prices add shine to Mitsui Mining shares.
newsitem.headline: High zinc prices add shine to Mitsui Mining shares.

text.p: Strong zinc prices, which hit a fresh seven-year high overnight, are adding shine to shares in Mitsui Mining and Smelting Co, Japan's largest zinc smelter, analysts said on Friday.
"Zinc has been very strong recently. In Japan, zinc means Mitsui," said Minoru Hasegawa, an analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Tokyo. "Our target is 600 yen."
Shares in Mitsui Mining climbed as high as 547 yen in the morning, setting a high for this year, compared with the previous 1997 high of 536 yen set on May 6.

The rise in Mitsui Mining's shares followed a surge in zinc prices on the London Metal Exchange overnight, taking the price of benchmark three-month zinc to $1,588 per tonne, a fresh seven-year high. In January the price was near $1,000.
Mitsui Mining said earlier on Friday that it had raised its selling price for zinc by 10,000 yen to 228,000 yen per tonne. It is the fourth time this month that Mitsui Mining has raised the price.
"Mitsui is likely to revise upwards its profits outlook. It has said it expected the international zinc price to average around $1,150 this year," Deutsche Morgan's Hasegawa said.
Analysts said the sharp rise in international zinc prices since the beginning of this year would more than offset a decline of about 10 percent in zinc treatment charges this year.
Jiro Iokibe, an analyst at Daiwa Institute of Research, calculated that a rise of $100 in the metal's price would boost Mitsui's profit by about 400 million yen a year.
Analysts said the metal's price surge comes at a time when foreign investors have started to look at new sectors after profiting from rises in blue-chip stocks.

Other Japanese smelters were not as well positioned to benefit from the metal's performance on the LME as their zinc output was not as large, the analysts said, adding the country's other main smelter Mitsubishi Materials Corp had already stopped producing zinc.
Daiwa's Iokibe added: "A weaker yen benefits the non-ferrous metals sector in general. But Mitsui is a company which is very active in hedging its foreign exchange."
He added: "It's now almost certain they've locked in profits from a 10 yen fall against the dollar. A one-yen change in the dollar/yen rate means a profit of 200 million yen for them."

The rise in Mitsui's shares comes as no surprise to stock analysts who have been bullish on Mitsui for a while, as it has succeeded in diversifying into very profitable businesses, such as copper foil and materials for liquid crystal displays (LCDs). -- Tokyo Commodities Desk +81-3-3432-6179
